answer: Well, when you think about why Genesis starts with God and not with people, I would say first of all that the Bible never tries to argue that God exists, it just says it, and that already shows He is the eternal reality behind everything. And then, as I was reading, I noticed that Genesis 1:1 separates the Creator from the creature, so the heavens and the earth depend on Him while He does not depend on them at all. That means the whole story, before Adam or Noah or Abraham, has God at the center, and I think that is the point, that people are not the starting place of the story, God is, and everything else receives its existence from Him.

So the way I understand dominion and stewardship is this, and I think the lesson makes the same point: dominion is not something we own, it is authority that has been handed to us by God, delegated authority, so we are responsible to cultivate and protect and develop creation wisely, because the earth still belongs to Him and not to us. Exploitation is what happens when people act as if there were no higher Owner at all, using the world only for themselves, but stewardship is using the same authority while knowing we must give an account and showing care for what we have been given.

The serpent is very clever in Genesis 3, and I think what he does is come at it from two sides at once. First he questions what God actually said, and then he flatly contradicts the warning about death, so he is attacking whether God's word can be trusted. But at the same time he suggests that God is holding something back, that God is being restrictive and does not want them to have something good, and that attacks God's character, His goodness. So the temptation makes rebellion look like freedom, like liberation, when really it is a lie about both what God said and who God is.

I have to say this one took me a while to think through, but what I see is that Genesis 5 keeps saying "and he died" over and over, generation after generation, and that repetition is not an accident, because the warning back in chapters 2 and 3 has now become the ordinary reality of human life, and even a very long life of nine hundred years does not cancel death. Then Enoch is different, he walked with God and was not, because God took him, so in the middle of all that dying there is a sign that God is able to deliver a person from death.

I think when Genesis says Enoch walked with God it is describing a settled way of living, a direction of life, and it is not just a few religious moments when things get hard. He lived aware of God, in faith and obedience and communion and depending on God all the time, and Hebrews 11 confirms this by connecting him to faith and saying he pleased God. So to walk with God is to live every day before Him in that stable way, and it does not mean we never struggle or that we become perfect, only that our whole life is oriented toward Him.

When I think about how faith and obedience fit together in Abraham leaving, I notice first that Genesis 12:4 says Abram went as the Lord had told him, and he did not even have the destination yet or a complete map, which says to me that real faith is more than agreeing with true statements about God, it actually changes the direction a person's life takes. At the same time I would not say his obedience paid for the promise, because the promise was God's gift, so obedience is how his trust showed itself, and not a payment he made to earn anything.

So about the ram, what I would say after reading the chapter a couple of times is that Abraham offers the ram instead of his son, in the place of his son, so the substitution is stated right in the text, and Isaac is spared while another life is given in his place. In the chapter itself it is first of all God's immediate provision that protects the promised son, but then as you follow the whole Bible this pattern of one life given in the place of another grows through the sacrifices until it points forward to Christ, which is why the ram matters so much.

Joseph's family was already divided, and then Jacob loved Joseph more than the others and gave him a special robe, and I think that made the brothers jealous, they hated him, they could not speak peacefully to him. But I do not think the favoritism of Jacob lets the brothers off the hook, because each of them was still responsible for what he did, even if they were treated unfairly, and Genesis shows how partiality in a family can feed hatred without taking away anyone's personal responsibility for violence.

I think the main thing the lesson wants us to see is that theology does not begin with us searching around for God, it begins with God deciding to make Himself known. The reason is that the finite simply cannot reach the Infinite, a creature cannot climb up to the Creator by being clever or working hard at it, and if God had chosen to stay hidden then He could not have been known by anybody at all, so His self-disclosure is necessary, it is the only way we can have true knowledge of Him, and we should be thankful that He did reveal Himself to us.

Both words describe things the Holy Spirit does, but they are different, and I would explain it like this. Inspiration is what the Spirit did to make Scripture, because holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, so the text itself is God-breathed, and that work is finished since the Bible is complete. Illumination, on the other hand, is something the Spirit keeps doing now, enabling a believer to understand and apply the Word that was already written, so it is ongoing, and without it we may read the words but not grasp their meaning.

One of the attributes that God has that we do not share is immutability, and what that means, as I understand it, is that God does not change, not in His essence, not in His character and not in His promises either. Malachi 3:6 says it clearly when it says "I am the LORD, I do not change," and I find that very comforting, because the same God who comforted people long ago is the same God who comforts a believer today, so He is not different from what He was even by a little, which sets Him apart from everything He made.

The question is why Jesus had to go back up and not just stay here, and as I remember the unit it gives some reasons. One is that He ascended so that He could speak for us as our Advocate and Intercessor at the right hand of God, so that we have someone representing us before the Father, and another reason is that He had promised to send the Holy Spirit and said it was for our good that He go away, so the Spirit could come, and that is what His place at the right hand accomplishes in the end.

Regeneration is what the Bible calls the new birth, it is the Spirit giving life to a person who is spiritually dead, and this is exactly what total depravity requires, because total depravity says that the sinner is dead in sin and not able to come to God by himself, so the new birth is necessary for the simple reason that a dead person cannot give himself life, and no amount of effort or religion or good works on his part can do what only the Spirit does by making him a new creation.

These two truths seem like they pull against each other, but the lesson says both are true of every human at the same time. On one hand each person is made in the image of God, and that gives inherent dignity, a worth that is not earned and cannot be erased no matter what they do. On the other hand sin has reached every part of a person, the mind, the will, the emotions, which is what total depravity means, so none of us can save ourselves. So we honor every person as God's image-bearer while we also admit that every person, including ourselves, needs grace.

The lesson talks about two representative men, which are the first Adam and then Christ, whom it calls the last Adam. Adam failed, he disobeyed, and his disobedience brought ruin on the whole race that he represented and it distorted the image of God in us. Christ succeeds exactly where Adam fell because He obeyed perfectly, and His obedience is credited to those who are in Him, bringing righteousness and life, so that in the end the image of God is restored in His people through Him.

So there are two kinds of sin that the lesson separates, and the first is a sin of commission, which is doing the thing that we ought not do, an actual wrong that was committed, for example lying or stealing or speaking cruelly to somebody. The second kind is a sin of omission, which is failing to do the good that we ought to do, the right action that was left undone, for example refusing to help a person in need or staying silent when we should have spoken up, and both of them are real sins before God even if people only notice the first kind.

I think what the statement is doing is turning around the way most people naturally think, which is that God saves the people who deserve it. A reward is something a person is owed because of how well he performed, but a gift is given freely to somebody who has not earned it, and salvation is the second kind of thing, it is not payment to the righteous for their goodness, it is a gift to the guilty, who deserve nothing, and that is why it is called grace and why nobody can boast.

The mission of the church goes in three directions according to the lesson. Upward is worship, because the church exists first to glorify and adore God. Inward is fellowship and edification, which means believers build one another up and care for each other and grow in maturity together. And outward is evangelism, taking the gospel to those who have not heard it. All three are necessary, I think, because a church that only worships can become inward-looking and a church that only evangelizes can become shallow, so health needs all three together.

The difference, in my own words, is that uniformity would be everyone doing everything exactly the same, looking the same and worshiping the same and practicing the same with no differences whatsoever, while unity is a deeper oneness in the essentials of the faith that is able to hold together real diversity in secondary matters. This matters for denominations because it means that differences among denominations do not necessarily show disunity, since believers can be one body, with one Spirit and one Lord, while still differing on secondary things.

Exegesis means drawing the meaning out of the text, so that what the author intended is what controls the interpretation, while eisegesis is the opposite, which means reading into the passage whatever I already think or want it to say. The reason the lesson says every pastor faces the choice on Monday morning is that sermon preparation begins then, and you cannot avoid choosing: if you do not deliberately choose to do exegesis, then you will end up with eisegesis by default, because without discipline our own ideas fill the gap.

The way I remember it, the lesson suggests a sort of order for a pastor to follow on Monday morning, and it begins with prayer, praying over the passage before anything else, then reading it carefully, and after that studying its context, asking honest questions of the text, comparing it with other Scripture, and only at the very end applying it. So the steps go from prayer and reading toward context and questions, and application comes last, which is the important thing, that you do not jump to application before you understand.

God's name never appears anywhere in the book of Esther, which you would think is a problem, but the lesson says that this silence is itself the key to reading the book. It is deliberate, because God is hidden but still present, and He works through providence behind every scene, like the king's insomnia and the banquets and the timing of everything, so when you read the whole book at the book level it teaches that the God who is not named is still the one ruling, even when He seems absent.

On the first Easter two disheartened disciples were walking the road to Emmaus when a stranger, who was the risen Jesus, came alongside them, and starting with Moses and all the Prophets He explained in all the Scriptures the things about Himself. The lesson calls it the most important hermeneutics lesson ever given because Jesus Himself shows how to read the Bible, which is that all of Scripture points to Him, so that is the key for the pastor too.

There are three signals that the lesson names for finding the main point of a parable. The first is the question or situation that caused Jesus to tell it in the first place. The second is the audience, who it was that He was speaking to. The third is the climax of the story, where the weight of it falls. If you read the three together then you stay with the one central point of the parable and you do not wander off into the scenery and details of it.

The difference, as I understand it from the lesson, is that literal interpretation means taking the words in the sense that the author actually intended, and sometimes the author intended a figure of speech, so when Jesus says "I am the door" we read it literally by taking His intended figure. Literalistic interpretation is different, because it flattens everything down to the bare physical meaning of the words and ignores that the author may have meant a figure, so it would make Jesus a piece of wood. That is why they are not synonyms, even though people often use the two words as if they meant the same.

The three questions that the pastor should ask are the following, as best I can say. The first is what the speaker actually meant when he said it. The second is whether a flat literal reading of the words would produce an absurdity. And the third is whether this is a figure of speech or a literal statement of reality. Asking these three things keeps the pastor in between the two ditches, so that he reads each text in the sense the author intended, whether that is figurative or literal.

Reni painted a picture up in a dome, and the painting was so high up that nobody could see it clearly, but they set a mirror below it and in the mirror the image could be seen plainly. In the same way the Father is far above us and kind of hazy until we look into Christ, who is the mirror in which the Father's character is reflected, so that whoever has seen Christ has seen the Father clearly, and that is how Christ functions as the mirror.

The three preparations for the fullness of time were these. First there was the Greek language, because ever since Alexander the Great the common Greek was spoken across the empire, so the apostles could be understood just about everywhere and the New Testament was written in Greek. Second were the Roman roads and the peace that the Romans kept, so that people could travel safely. And third were the Jewish synagogues scattered through the empire, which gave the missionaries a place to begin in each city.

For the second century I would name Justin Martyr, who wrote the First Apology, defending the Christians against the slanders of incest and cannibalism and who also wrote the Dialogue with Trypho, and Tertullian, who gave Western theology its Latin vocabulary, including the word Trinity and the formula of three persons in one substance. The third is Irenaeus, who defended the faith against the Gnostics, so each of these three made a main contribution in defending and explaining Christianity.

In the year 312 Constantine won the battle at the Milvian Bridge after seeing, according to Eusebius, a cross of light in the sky, and he credited his victory to the God of the Christians and became the protector of the Church. Then the Edict of Milan in 313 granted Christians freedom of worship, gave back the property that had been confiscated and ended the persecution, so the two events together changed the position of the church in the Roman Empire completely.

The four councils in order are these. Nicaea in 325, which condemned Arius and affirmed that the Son is homoousios, of the same substance as the Father. Then Constantinople in 381, which confirmed Nicaea and confessed the full deity of the Holy Spirit, finishing the doctrine of the Trinity. Then Ephesus in 431, which condemned Nestorius and affirmed Mary as theotokos. And last Chalcedon in 451, which defined that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human.

Augustine's grace doctrine as I recall is about the following points, which have shaped the West. There is original sin, since in Adam all fell. There is the bondage of the will, that the unredeemed will is enslaved to its disordered loves. There is prevenient grace, which means grace comes before any decision by the sinner and even faith is a gift. And there is the necessity of grace for salvation, so that without it no one can come to God or persevere.

Luther was a monk who was tormented and could not find peace through confession and penance, so Staupitz sent him to teach the Bible at Wittenberg. Studying Romans 1:17, "the just shall live by faith," he came to understand about 1515, in the tower of the Black Cloister, that the righteousness of God is not the standard that condemns us but a gift that is received by faith, and that discovery freed him and led to the Reformation.

William Carey was a shoemaker in Northamptonshire and a self-taught linguist who became pastor of a small congregation. Against the hyper-Calvinists who held that the Great Commission was given only to the apostles, he published his Enquiry in 1792, arguing that Christians were obliged to use means to spread the gospel, and then he went to India himself, so he is called the father of modern missions because he started the modern missionary movement.

The reason Psalm 1 is called the threshold psalm, I think, is that it stands right at the doorway of the entire book of Psalms like a porch you walk across to enter a house. It introduces the theme that is found all the way through, that there are only two ways to live, the way of the righteous who delight in the Word of God and are like a fruitful tree, and the way of the wicked, and so the choice it sets before every reader is which of those two ways they will walk.

In the valley of the shadow of death Psalm 23 promises the presence of God. It says "I will fear no evil, for You are with me," but it does not promise that we will be spared the valley itself, we may still walk through it. David is an example, because when he faced Goliath God did not remove the giant but gave David courage and help to face him, and so the psalm promises God with us in the valley and not a life without any valley.

The story behind Psalm 24 is in 2 Samuel 6, where David brings the Ark of God up to Jerusalem. The first attempt failed because they carried the Ark on a new ox cart, not as God had commanded, and when the cart shook Uzzah reached out to steady the Ark and died. So what that teaches us about approaching God is that we must come to Him in the way He has commanded, with reverence, and not simply in whatever manner seems good to us.

What makes Psalm 119 unique is, first of all, its length, since it is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with 176 verses, and second its structure, because it is a carefully made acrostic poem with twenty-two sections, one section for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every verse in a section begins with that same letter, so it is both the longest chapter and the most orderly in its design.

Psalm 22:1 opens with "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" and these are the very words that Jesus cried from the cross. The lesson says that this was the deepest pain of the crucifixion, deeper than the nails or the mockery, because while the physical agony was terrible, the worst was the forsakenness, the moment that the Son bore the sin of the world, so that is why the cry is so important.

The sixth benefit that is mentioned is that God renews our strength, so that our youth is renewed like the eagle's. The lesson is careful to say that this has nothing to do with age and is not about staying physically young, which is what the world is always searching for. It is the inner renewal that Isaiah promised, that those who wait on the LORD will renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles, so it is an inner strength given by God.

The warning for ministers, using the tree of Psalm 1, is that the tree bears fruit only because its roots stay buried deep beside the rivers of water. The danger for trained ministers is letting private devotion shrink while their public skill grows, so they become more and more capable in public while the hidden root withers, and the lesson says that no amount of public ability can replace those roots, so a minister must keep his private time with God.

Apologia is a Greek word and it was used in the courtroom, it meant the reasoned defense that a person made for himself when someone demanded to know why. Peter takes that legal word in 1 Peter 3:15 and applies it to every believer, saying to always be ready to give an answer, a reason, for the hope in us. So it teaches that defending the faith with reasons is the responsibility of every believer, not only of pastors or experts.

General revelation is what everyone has of God through creation and conscience, as in Psalm 19 where the heavens declare His glory and in Romans 2 where the conscience accuses or excuses us, and together they make it plain that God exists and that we are accountable, so that people are without excuse. But it is not enough to save, because the heavens can tell me God is powerful but not that He is merciful, and my conscience says I did wrong but not how it is forgiven, so more is needed.

The unit's free-will answer to the problem of evil is that God allowed the possibility of evil for the sake of love. He could have made puppets that could never sin, moving only as He pulled the strings, but a puppet cannot love, because forced love is no love. If He wanted creatures who could truly love Him, He had to make them free, and a freedom that cannot choose against the good is not freedom at all, so the same door that allowed love also allowed sin.

The fingerprint of prophecy is what the unit calls the pre-written biography of the Messiah, which the prophets sketched centuries before He was born. Micah named Bethlehem as the place of His birth seven hundred years early, Psalm 22 described death by the piercing of hands and feet and casting lots for clothing before crucifixion even existed, and Isaiah 53 drew the suffering servant. These are specific, not vague horoscopes, and they all point to one life, Jesus.

The unit looks at the natural alternatives to the resurrection and shows that each has serious difficulties. If the disciples stole the body, they would not have died for what they knew was a fraud. If Jesus only swooned and revived, then a man who was flogged and pierced through the heart could not have rolled away the stone, overpowered the guards and convinced his followers of victory. So the conclusion is that "He rose" is the best explanation of the evidence.

In John 14:6, when Thomas asked how they could know the way, Jesus did not give directions but said "I am the way, the truth, and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Me." The unit calls it the most offensive verse because in a world that puts tolerance above everything, such an exclusive claim hurts, but Jesus is not being unkind, He is simply telling us the truth about how we reach the Father.

The quiet refrain throughout the course is that the evidence can carry a person to the door but cannot drag him through it. The heavens show a Designer, the tomb a risen Lord, the documents a trustworthy record, and they take away excuses, but the last step is a movement of the will and a bowing of the heart that no argument can do. This guards against two errors, trusting in your own cleverness instead of the Spirit and carrying a burden that was never yours.
